sections.title: Lewis Concept of Acids and Bases

blocks.t: Section 9.2 (pp.187-188) is removed from the smart syllabus. Lewis acid-base theory (electron-pair donor/acceptor) is NOT tested.
Pure water is a poor conductor of electricity, but its conductance is measurable. Water undergoes self-ionization reversibly — it is a weak electrolyte that ionizes to a limited extent.

H₂O(l)  +  H₂O(l)  ⇌  H₃O⁺(aq)  +  OH⁻(aq)
Net:  H₂O(l)  ⇌  H⁺(aq)  +  OH⁻(aq)

blocks.head: Derivation of Kw
blocks.body: The equilibrium constant Kc for water ionization is:
blocks.eq:
Kc = [H⁺][OH⁻] / [H₂O] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁶

Moles of H₂O in 1 litre = 1000/18 = 55.5 mol dm⁻³

Since [H₂O] is constant (large excess), it is merged with Kc:
Kc × [H₂O] = [H⁺][OH⁻]  =  Kw
blocks.note: Kw is also called the dissociation constant of water.

blocks.label: Ionic Product of Water (Kw)
blocks.text: Kw is called ionic product of water or dissociation constant of water.

blocks.head: Effect of Adding Acid or Base
blocks.body: When acid or base is added, Kw stays constant at 10⁻¹⁴, but [H⁺] and [OH⁻] change:

blocks.t: The ionization of water is an endothermic process. When temperature increases, Kw increases (Le Chatelier's principle shifts equilibrium right).

blocks.caption: Graph of Kw vs temperature showing increase from 0°C to 100°C
blocks.alt: Line graph showing Kw increasing with temperature, with values from table above marked

blocks.t: Board question: 'Why does Kw increase with temperature?' Answer: Water ionization is endothermic. Higher temperature shifts equilibrium right, increasing [H⁺] and [OH⁻] and therefore Kw. At 100°C, Kw is ~75 times the value at 0°C.

items.q: Equal volumes of pH 4.0 and pH 10.0 solutions are mixed. Calculate Kw at 25°C.
items.ans: Answer: Kw is a temperature-dependent constant — it does not change with mixing. At 25°C, Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ regardless of what solutions are mixed, as long as temperature stays at 25°C.

items.q: Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹³ at a certain temperature. [OH⁻] = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ M. Find [H⁺] and pH.
items.ans:
Step 1 — Find [H⁺]:

Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] 1.0 × 10⁻¹³ = [H⁺] × 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹³ / 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ = 4.0 × 10⁻⁹ M

Step 2 — Find pH:

pH = −log(4.0 × 10⁻⁹) = 9 − log 4 = 9 − 0.60 = 8.40

items.q: Concentrated HNO₃ is diluted to 0.30 M. Find [H⁺], pH, [OH⁻] and pOH at 25°C.
items.ans:
HNO₃ is a strong acid — fully dissociates:

[H⁺] = 0.30 mol dm⁻³ pH = −log(0.30) = 0.52 [OH⁻] = Kw / [H⁺] = 10⁻¹⁴ / 0.30 = 3.33 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol dm⁻³ pOH = 14 − 0.52 = 13.48

blocks.t: In 1909, Sorenson (a Danish biochemist) introduced the pH and pOH scales. [H⁺] and [OH⁻] values are extremely small (negative powers of 10), so we take the negative logarithm to convert them into convenient positive numbers.

blocks.label: pH
blocks.text: pH is the negative logarithm of molar concentration of H⁺ ions.

blocks.label: pOH
blocks.text: pOH is the negative logarithm of molar concentration of OH⁻ ions.

blocks.t:
pH  = −log[H⁺]
pOH = −log[OH⁻]
pH + pOH = 14  (at 25°C)

blocks.head: pH Scale Summary
blocks.body: As pH increases: pOH decreases, acidic strength decreases, basic strength increases.
blocks.note: Acidic strength ∝ 1/pH — lower pH means stronger acid.

blocks.caption: pH scale showing common substances from 0 (battery acid) to 14 (NaOH). Stomach: 1–3, vinegar: 2.4–3.4, blood: ~7.4
blocks.alt: Horizontal colour-coded pH scale from 0 (red, acidic) through 7 (green, neutral) to 14 (blue, basic) with common substances labelled

blocks.t: Common board data: pH of stomach (pepsin) = 1.0–3.0, vinegar = 2.4–3.4, blood = ~7.4. Solutions with negative pH and pH > 14 do exist (very concentrated acids/bases).

blocks.head: Sample Problem 9.1 — Finding Kw from pH
blocks.body: pH = 9.2 in a solution at 25°C. Find Kw.

blocks.t: Acids dissolved in water may dissociate completely (strong acids) or only partially (weak acids). The acid dissociation constant Ka is the equilibrium constant for this dissociation and measures how strong the acid is.

blocks.label: Acid Dissociation Constant (Ka)
blocks.text: Ka is the dissociation constant of an acid — it is the quantitative measure of the strength of the acid.

blocks.t:
HA + H₂O  ⇌  H₃O⁺  +  A⁻

Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻] / [HA]

([H₂O] is omitted — it is in large excess and stays constant)

blocks.head: Acid Strength from Ka
blocks.body: Acidic strength ∝ extent of ionization ∝ Ka. Larger Ka = stronger acid, smaller Ka = weaker acid.

blocks.head: BOOK ERROR — Page 192, Table 9.3 (H₂CO₃ row)
blocks.wrong: Table shows H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HS⁻ with Ka = 4.4 × 10⁻⁷
blocks.reason: HS⁻ is the conjugate base of H₂S, not H₂CO₃. The conjugate base of carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) is bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻). The Ka value of 4.4 × 10⁻⁷ correctly belongs to H₂CO₃. The table row uses the correct Ka but the wrong conjugate base.

blocks.head: BOOK ERROR — Page 192, Table 9.3 (NH₄⁺ row)
blocks.reason: NH₅ does not exist. When NH₄⁺ (ammonium ion) donates a proton, the product is NH₃ (ammonia), not NH₅. The charge on NH₄ (should be NH₄⁺) is also missing.

blocks.t: 9.5.1 Calculating H₃O⁺ Concentration from Ka
Weak acids ionize to a limited extent, so [H₃O⁺] is much less than the initial acid concentration C. We use the ICE (Initial–Change–Equilibrium) method, then apply an approximation.

blocks.head: ICE Table Derivation
blocks.body: For weak acid HA with initial concentration C mol dm⁻³:
blocks.eq:
HA     ⇌    H₃O⁺  +   A⁻
I:         C               0          0
C:       −x             +x        +x
E:     C − x             x          x

Ka = x² / (C − x)
Since x << C,  C − x ≈ C
∴ Ka ≈ x²/C
∴ x = [H₃O⁺] = √(Ka × C)
blocks.note: This approximation is valid when Ka << C (less than ~5% ionization).

blocks.t: Board shortcut: [H₃O⁺] = √(Ka × C) for any weak acid. Example: 0.1 M CH₃COOH, Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ → [H₃O⁺] = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.34 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³.

items.q: pH of 0.10 M formic acid (HCOOH) at 25°C is 2.38. Calculate Ka.
items.ans:
Step 1 — Find [H⁺]:

[H⁺] = 10⁻²·³⁸ = 4.17 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³

Step 2 — Find Ka:

Ka = [H⁺]² / ([HA] − [H⁺]) = (4.17 × 10⁻³)² / (0.10 − 4.17 × 10⁻³) = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ / 0.0958 ≈ 1.8 × 10⁻⁴

items.q: Calculate [H₃O⁺] in 0.1 M HNO₂ solution. Ka = 4 × 10⁻⁴.
Vinegar: 0.837 M CH₃COOH, [H₃O⁺] = 3.86 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. Find Ka.

blocks.label: Common Ion Effect
blocks.text: The suppression of ionization of a weak electrolyte by adding a common ion to it is called common ion effect.

blocks.t: Adding a common ion (an ion already present in the equilibrium mixture) from an external source increases its concentration. By Le Chatelier's principle, equilibrium shifts left — ionization of the weak electrolyte is suppressed and more of it stays in un-ionized form, which may precipitate out.

items.title: Purification of NaCl (Brine Method)
items.body: — NaCl saturated solution (brine) is treated with HCl gas. HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻. Cl⁻ is the common ion. Excess Cl⁻ shifts NaCl equilibrium left: Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → NaCl(s). Pure NaCl crystallizes out.

items.title: Group II Salt Analysis (H₂S method)
items.body: — HCl provides H⁺ (common ion to H₂S). Suppresses H₂S ionization: H₂S ⇌ 2H⁺ + S²⁻. Low [S²⁻] ensures only Group II cations (Cu²⁺, Cd²⁺, Sn²⁺) precipitate as sulfides.

items.title: Group III Salt Analysis (NH₄Cl + NH₃)
items.body: — NH₄Cl provides NH₄⁺ (common ion to NH₃). Suppresses NH₃ ionization, reducing [OH⁻]. Controlled [OH⁻] ensures only Group III cations precipitate as hydroxides.

items.title: Suppression of KClO₃ ionization
items.body: — Adding KCl to KClO₃ solution. K⁺ is the common ion. KClO₃ precipitates out of solution.

rxns.eq: NaCl(s) ⇌ Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)  ← HCl adds more Cl⁻ → NaCl precipitates
H₂S(g) ⇌ 2H⁺(aq) + S²⁻(aq)  ← HCl adds H⁺ → ionization suppressed

NH₄Cl(aq) → NH₄⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)
NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)  ← NH₄⁺ suppresses OH⁻ production

blocks.t: Board question: 'What effect does adding NaCl have on the solubility of AgCl?' Cl⁻ is the common ion — AgCl solubility decreases. Common ion effect = Le Chatelier's principle in action.

blocks.label: Buffer Solution
blocks.text: The solutions which resist the change in their pH when a small amount of an acid or a base is added to them, are called buffer solutions.

blocks.t: A buffer works on the principle of Le Chatelier's principle and common ion effect. Its pH does not change even on dilution and remains stable for a long time.

rows: Weak acid + salt of weak acid with strong base
Weak base + salt of weak base with strong acid

blocks.t: How Acidic Buffer Works — CH₃COOH + CH₃COONa

CH₃COONa completely dissociates, providing a large reservoir of CH₃COO⁻. This common ion suppresses CH₃COOH dissociation. The solution has high concentrations of both CH₃COOH (weak acid) and CH₃COO⁻ (conjugate base).

rxns.note: Salt — fully dissociates, provides CH₃COO⁻ (common ion)

blocks.head: Buffer Action — How pH is Maintained
blocks.body: The buffer has a large reservoir of both CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻:
items: Add H⁺ (acid): CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH — extra H⁺ absorbed, pH barely changes.
Add OH⁻ (base): CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O — base neutralized, pH barely changes.

blocks.caption: Reservoir model of buffer: large pool of weak acid and conjugate base absorbing added H⁺ or OH⁻ without significant pH change
blocks.alt: Two arrows showing added H+ absorbed by A- on left and added OH- absorbed by HA on right, with a large central reservoir

blocks.head: NOTE ERROR — Buffer Capacity
blocks.wrong: Notes state buffer capacity 'depends on polarity'
blocks.correct: Buffer capacity depends on the concentrations (molar amounts) of the weak acid and conjugate base in the buffer. Higher concentrations → greater buffer capacity.
blocks.reason: Polarity is a property related to bond dipole moments and has nothing to do with how much acid or base a buffer can absorb. Buffer capacity is purely a function of concentration.

blocks.t: 9.7.1 Henderson's Equation — Calculating Buffer pH

blocks.head: Derivation of Henderson's Equation
blocks.body: Start from the Ka expression for weak acid HA:
blocks.eq:
Ka = [H⁺][A⁻] / [HA]
[H⁺] = Ka × [HA] / [A⁻]

Take −log of both sides:
pH = pKa − log([HA]/[A⁻])

Interchange numerator and denominator (sign flips):
pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA])
pH = pKa + log([Salt]/[Acid])
blocks.note: This is Henderson's equation. [Salt] = [A⁻] = conjugate base concentration.

blocks.label: Henderson's Equation
blocks.text: pH = pKa + log([Salt]/[Acid]) — used to calculate the pH of a buffer solution.

blocks.head: Special Case: [Salt] = [Acid]
blocks.body: When concentrations of salt and acid are equal:
blocks.eq:
pH = pKa + log(1)
pH = pKa + 0
pH = pKa
blocks.note: The best buffer is prepared with equal concentrations — pH equals pKa of the acid. For CH₃COOH/CH₃COONa buffer: pH = pKa = 4.74.

blocks.t: Henderson's equation: pH = pKa + log([Salt]/[Acid]). Key rule: when [Salt] = [Acid], pH = pKa. More salt → higher pH. More acid → lower pH.

items.q: Explain the impact of common ion effect on solubility.
items.ans: Adding a common ion disturbs the equilibrium of a sparingly soluble salt. By Le Chatelier's principle, the equilibrium shifts left — more of the salt precipitates out. This decreases the solubility of the salt, while Ksp remains constant.

items.q: NaCl solution is added to saturated AgCl. (i) Effect on [Ag⁺]? (ii) Explain with respect to common ion effect.
items.ans:
(i) [Ag⁺] decreases.

(ii) NaCl provides Cl⁻ — the common ion. AgCl ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻. The extra Cl⁻ shifts equilibrium left. Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ combine to form more AgCl precipitate. [Ag⁺] falls to maintain constant Ksp.

items.q: How does a buffer maintain pH stability?
items.ans:
A buffer contains a large reservoir of weak acid and its conjugate base:

  • When H⁺ is added: A⁻ + H⁺ → HA (conjugate base absorbs extra H⁺)
  • When OH⁻ is added: HA + OH⁻ → A⁻ + H₂O (weak acid neutralizes the base)

Both processes consume the added H⁺ or OH⁻ without significantly changing [H⁺], so pH stays almost constant.

items.q: Calculate pH of 0.50 M HF / 0.45 M F⁻ buffer. Ka(HF) = 6.8 × 10⁻⁴. Then add 0.40 g NaOH to 1.0 dm³.
items.ans:
Before addition:

pKa = −log(6.8 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.17 pH = 3.17 + log(0.45/0.50) = 3.17 − 0.046 = 3.12

After adding NaOH: mol NaOH = 0.40/40 = 0.010 mol

New [HF] = 0.50 − 0.010 = 0.49 M New [F⁻] = 0.45 + 0.010 = 0.46 M pH = 3.17 + log(0.46/0.49) = 3.17 − 0.027 = 3.14

pH changed only slightly (3.12 → 3.14), demonstrating buffer action.

items.q: Calculate pH of buffer: 0.11 M CH₃COONa and 0.09 M CH₃COOH. Ka = 1.85 × 10⁻⁵.

blocks.t: When a sparingly soluble (slightly soluble) ionic salt is added to water, only a tiny amount dissolves. An equilibrium exists between the undissolved solid and the dissolved ions. The solubility product Ksp describes this equilibrium.

blocks.label: Solubility Product (Ksp)
blocks.text: Ksp is the product of the concentrations of ions raised to an exponent equal to the coefficient of the balanced equation.

blocks.head: Derivation — PbSO₄
blocks.body: Since [PbSO₄] (solid) is essentially constant, it is merged with Kc:
blocks.eq:
PbSO₄(s)  ⇌  Pb²⁺(aq)  +  SO₄²⁻(aq)

Kc = [Pb²⁺][SO₄²⁻] / [PbSO₄]
Kc × [PbSO₄] = [Pb²⁺][SO₄²⁻] = Ksp

Ksp = [Pb²⁺][SO₄²⁻] = 1.6 × 10⁻⁸  at 25°C

blocks.head: PbCl₂ — Coefficients Become Exponents
blocks.body: When the coefficient in the balanced equation is > 1, it becomes an exponent in Ksp:

blocks.head: Key Facts About Ksp
blocks.body: Important rules to remember for board exams:
items: Ksp applies only to sparingly soluble (weak electrolyte) salts — not to fully soluble salts like NaCl.
Ksp is temperature-dependent. It does NOT change when concentrations change.
Ksp tells us the extent of ionization during dissolution.

blocks.t: 9.8.1 Applications of Solubility Product
a) Calculating Solubility from Ksp
Set up an ICE table using molar solubility S. Express ion concentrations in terms of S, substitute into Ksp, and solve for S.
b) Common Ion Effect and Solubility
The presence of a common ion decreases the solubility of a slightly soluble ionic compound. Adding a common ion shifts equilibrium left — more solid precipitates while Ksp remains constant.

blocks.head: NOTE ERROR — Common Ion Effect on Ksp
blocks.wrong: Notes state: 'Common ion effect decreases Ksp (with increase in concentration)'
blocks.correct: Common ion effect decreases SOLUBILITY. Ksp is a constant at a given temperature and is NOT changed by the common ion effect.
blocks.reason: Ksp changes only with temperature. Adding a common ion shifts the equilibrium left, so less salt dissolves (solubility decreases), but the value of Ksp itself is unchanged.

blocks.head: Example — Na₂CrO₄ added to PbCrO₄ solution
blocks.body: Saturated PbCrO₄ equilibrium with Na₂CrO₄ added:
blocks.eq:
PbCrO₄(s)  ⇌  Pb²⁺(aq)  +  CrO₄²⁻(aq)

Na₂CrO₄ dissolves → provides CrO₄²⁻ (common ion)
Excess CrO₄²⁻ shifts equilibrium left
→ More PbCrO₄ precipitates
→ [Pb²⁺] decreases, Ksp stays constant

blocks.t: c) Predicting Precipitation
The ionic product Qc (product of actual ion concentrations at that moment) is compared to Ksp to predict whether a precipitate will form:

blocks.head: Sample Problem — CaSO₄ Precipitation
blocks.body: Ksp(CaSO₄) = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵. Mix 10⁻² mol dm⁻³ Ca²⁺ with 10⁻² mol dm⁻³ SO₄²⁻.
blocks.eq:
[Ca²⁺] = [SO₄²⁻] = 10⁻² / 2 = 5.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³
Qc = (5.0 × 10⁻³)(5.0 × 10⁻³) = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵

Qc (2.5 × 10⁻⁵) > Ksp (2.0 × 10⁻⁵)
∴ CaSO₄ will precipitate out.

blocks.t: Board tip: Always compare Qc with Ksp, not the other way around. If Qc > Ksp → precipitation. If Qc < Ksp → no precipitation. Ksp is temperature-dependent only — adding ions does NOT change Ksp.

items.q: Ksp(AgCl) = 1.77 × 10⁻¹⁰. Find solubility of AgCl when 0.10 M NaCl is added.
items.ans:
NaCl provides Cl⁻ — the common ion. In presence of 0.10 M Cl⁻:

Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] 1.77 × 10⁻¹⁰ = [Ag⁺] × 0.10 [Ag⁺] = 1.77 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³

Solubility of AgCl = 1.77 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³ — much lower than in pure water (1.33 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³). This is common ion effect.

items.q: Will CaSO₄ precipitate when 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ each of Ca²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ are mixed? Ksp = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵.
Potassium carbonate solution is basic. (i) Why? (ii) Write the hydrolysis equation.
items.ans:
(i) K₂CO₃ → 2K⁺ + CO₃²⁻. CO₃²⁻ is the conjugate base of HCO₃⁻ (weak acid) and reacts with water, producing OH⁻ → solution is basic.

(ii)

CO₃²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HCO₃⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq)

mcqs.q: The pH of 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ of an aqueous solution of H₂SO₄ is:
mcqs.exp: H₂SO₄ is diprotic — each molecule releases 2 H⁺. [H⁺] = 2 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. pH = −log(2 × 10⁻³) = 3 − log 2 = 3 − 0.30 = 2.70.

mcqs.q: The solubility product of AgCl is 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol² dm⁻⁶. The maximum concentration of Ag⁺ ions in the solution is:
mcqs.exp: AgCl ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻. Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] = [Ag⁺]² (since [Ag⁺] = [Cl⁻] = S). S = √(2.0 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.41 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³.

mcqs.q: In an acid-base titration, the equivalence point is reached when:
opts: Equal volumes of acid and base have been added
mcqs.exp: The equivalence point is when stoichiometric amounts of acid and base have completely reacted. Option a (pH 7) is only true for strong acid–strong base. Option b describes the end point (indicator change). Option c requires equal concentrations too, not just equal volumes. Option d (reaction complete) best represents the equivalence condition.

mcqs.q: If the pH of a solution is 11, what is the [OH⁻] concentration in the solution?
Which of the following pairs forms a buffer solution?
mcqs.exp: A buffer requires a weak acid + its conjugate base salt (or weak base + conjugate acid salt). CH₃COOH (weak acid) + CH₃COONa (its sodium salt) is the classic acidic buffer. HCl and NaCl are both strong — not a buffer.

mcqs.q: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for an acidic buffer is:
mcqs.exp: Henderson's equation: pH = pKa + log([Salt]/[Acid]). It uses pKa (negative log of Ka) and the ratio of conjugate base (salt) to weak acid. More salt → higher pH.

mcqs.q: Ksp of a sparingly soluble salt changes when:
mcqs.exp: Ksp is temperature-dependent only. Adding a common ion, changing concentrations, or diluting do NOT change Ksp — they only change solubility.

mcqs.q: Which condition leads to precipitation from a slightly soluble salt solution?
mcqs.exp: When ionic product Qc exceeds Ksp, the solution is supersaturated and precipitation occurs to restore equilibrium (shift left).

mcqs.q: When HCl is passed into a saturated NaCl solution, NaCl crystallizes out because:
opts: Cl⁻ from HCl is the common ion
mcqs.exp: HCl provides Cl⁻ (common ion). The increased [Cl⁻] shifts the NaCl equilibrium left — Na⁺ and Cl⁻ combine to precipitate NaCl. This is common ion effect used to purify NaCl.

sqs.q: Define the following with an example for each: (i) Ionization constant (ii) Solubility product (iii) Common ion effect (iv) Acid-base indicator
sqs.a:
(i) Ionization Constant (Ka):

Ka is the quantitative measure of the strength of an acid — the equilibrium constant for its dissociation in water.

HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻ Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻] / [HA]

Example: Ka of CH₃COOH = 1.85 × 10⁻⁵. Larger Ka = stronger acid; smaller Ka = weaker acid.

(ii) Solubility Product (Ksp):

Ksp is the product of the molar concentrations of ions of a sparingly soluble salt, raised to the power of their stoichiometric coefficients, at equilibrium.

AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰

Smaller Ksp = less soluble salt. Ksp is temperature-dependent.

(iii) Common Ion Effect:

The suppression of ionization of a weak electrolyte by adding a common ion to it.

NaCl(s) ⇌ Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) Passing HCl adds Cl⁻ (common ion) → NaCl crystallizes out (NaCl purification)

(iv) Acid-Base Indicator: (Note: Section 9.10 is removed from smart syllabus — this part of SAQ a may not be tested.)

An indicator is a substance that changes colour to mark the endpoint of a titration. Most indicators are weak organic acids (HIn) with different colours in ionized (In⁻) and un-ionized (HIn) forms: HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻. Example: litmus (red in acid, blue in base). Example 2: phenolphthalein (colourless in acid, pink in base).

sqs.q: Differentiate between: (i) Hydrolysis and dissolution (ii) Acidic and basic buffer solutions
sqs.a:
(i) Hydrolysis vs Dissolution: (Note: Salt hydrolysis is from deleted section 9.9.)

  • Hydrolysis: Reaction of ions of a salt with water to produce an acidic or basic solution. Example: CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻ (basic solution).
  • Dissolution: Simple dissolving of a substance in water, without any chemical reaction with water. Example: NaCl → Na⁺ + Cl⁻. The solution remains neutral.

(ii) Acidic Buffer vs Basic Buffer:

  • Acidic Buffer: pH less than 7. Prepared by mixing a weak acid with its salt with a strong base. Example: CH₃COOH + CH₃COONa. The common ion is CH₃COO⁻.
  • Basic Buffer: pH greater than 7. Prepared by mixing a weak base with its salt with a strong acid. Example: NH₄OH + NH₄Cl. The common ion is NH₄⁺.
  • Both types resist change in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.

sqs.q: Which salt would you expect to dissolve more readily in acidic solution: BaCO₃ or CuS? Explain. [Ksp(BaCO₃) = 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰, Ksp(CuS) = 8 × 10⁻³⁴]
sqs.a:
Answer: BaCO₃ dissolves more readily in acidic solution.

For BaCO₃:

BaCO₃(s) ⇌ Ba²⁺(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq) Ksp = 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ In acidic solution: CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂↑

The acid consumes CO₃²⁻ (conjugate base of weak acid H₂CO₃). This shifts the BaCO₃ equilibrium right, dissolving more salt. Since Ksp is relatively large (10⁻¹⁰), BaCO₃ dissolves readily in acid.

For CuS:

CuS(s) ⇌ Cu²⁺(aq) + S²⁻(aq) Ksp = 8 × 10⁻³⁴ In acidic solution: S²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂S

Although acid does consume S²⁻, the Ksp of CuS is extremely small (8 × 10⁻³⁴). The equilibrium is so far left that even in acid, CuS barely dissolves.

Conclusion: BaCO₃ (Ksp = 10⁻¹⁰) dissolves more readily in acidic solution than CuS (Ksp = 10⁻³⁴).

sqs.q: Why does common ion effect decrease the solubility of a less soluble salt?
sqs.a:
Definition: The suppression of ionization of a weak electrolyte by adding a common ion is the common ion effect.

Mechanism — Example of AgCl:

AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰

If NaCl (source of Cl⁻) is added to this saturated solution, [Cl⁻] increases suddenly. The ionic product Qc = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] exceeds Ksp.

Le Chatelier's Principle: To restore equilibrium, the reaction shifts left — Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ combine and more AgCl precipitates. This reduces [Ag⁺], meaning less AgCl is dissolved — solubility decreases.

Conclusion: Adding a common ion shifts equilibrium toward the undissolved solid, reducing solubility while keeping Ksp constant (since Ksp is temperature-dependent, not concentration-dependent).

sqs.q: State the basic principle of solubility product. Mention factors affecting solubility product.
sqs.a:
Basic Principle:

When a sparingly soluble salt dissolves in water, it establishes equilibrium between undissolved solid and its dissolved ions. The product of ion concentrations (raised to stoichiometric coefficients) at equilibrium is a constant called Ksp.

AxBy(s) ⇌ xAʸ⁺(aq) + yBˣ⁻(aq) Ksp = [Aʸ⁺]ˣ [Bˣ⁻]ʸ

Example: PbSO₄ ⇌ Pb²⁺ + SO₄²⁻; Ksp = [Pb²⁺][SO₄²⁻] = 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ at 25°C.

Factors Affecting Ksp:

  • Temperature: Ksp is temperature-dependent. For most salts, Ksp increases with temperature (dissolution is endothermic).
  • Nature of solvent: Ksp changes if a different solvent is used.
  • NOT affected by: Adding common ions, changing pressure, or changing the amount of solid salt. These affect solubility, not Ksp.

sqs.q: Prove by equations what happens when Na₂CrO₄ is added to saturated solution of PbCrO₄.
sqs.a:
Step 1 — Saturated PbCrO₄ equilibrium:

PbCrO₄(s) ⇌ Pb²⁺(aq) + CrO₄²⁻(aq) Ksp = [Pb²⁺][CrO₄²⁻] = 2.3 × 10⁻¹³

Step 2 — Na₂CrO₄ is added:

Na₂CrO₄(aq) → 2Na⁺(aq) + CrO₄²⁻(aq)

Na₂CrO₄ is a soluble salt that completely dissociates. It provides CrO₄²⁻ — the common ion already present in the PbCrO₄ equilibrium.

Step 3 — Effect:

The added CrO₄²⁻ increases [CrO₄²⁻]. The ionic product Qc = [Pb²⁺][CrO₄²⁻] now exceeds Ksp. To restore Ksp, equilibrium shifts left — more PbCrO₄ precipitates. [Pb²⁺] decreases.

Conclusion: Adding Na₂CrO₄ to saturated PbCrO₄ increases [CrO₄²⁻], shifts equilibrium left, and causes more PbCrO₄ to precipitate. This is a demonstration of common ion effect reducing solubility.

sqs.q: If the concentration of hydrogen ions in a solution is 1 × 10⁻⁵ M, what is the pH of the solution?
sqs.a:
Given: [H⁺] = 1 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³

pH = −log[H⁺] pH = −log(1 × 10⁻⁵) pH = −(−5) pH = 5

Conclusion: pH = 5. Since pH < 7, the solution is acidic at 25°C.

sqs.q: Explain how an acidic buffer solution maintains its pH when a small amount of strong acid is added.
sqs.a:
Definition: A buffer solution resists change in pH when a small amount of acid or base is added. Its pH does not change on dilution.

Example — CH₃COOH + CH₃COONa buffer:

CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ (weak acid — partially dissociated) CH₃COONa → CH₃COO⁻ + Na⁺ (salt — fully dissociated, large [CH₃COO⁻])

When H⁺ (strong acid) is added:

CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) → CH₃COOH(aq)

The large reservoir of CH₃COO⁻ (conjugate base) absorbs the added H⁺, converting it to the weak acid CH₃COOH. Since CH₃COOH is a weak acid, it does not fully re-ionize — [H⁺] barely changes and pH remains stable.

Conclusion: The conjugate base (CH₃COO⁻) acts as an H⁺ sponge, neutralizing added acid without significant pH change.

sqs.q: Calculate the pH of a buffer containing 0.50 M CH₃COOH and 0.50 M CH₃COONa. Ka = 1.85 × 10⁻⁵.
sqs.a:
Given: [CH₃COOH] = 0.50 M, [CH₃COONa] = 0.50 M, Ka = 1.85 × 10⁻⁵

Step 1 — Find pKa:

pKa = −log(1.85 × 10⁻⁵) = 4.73

Step 2 — Apply Henderson's equation:

pH = pKa + log([Salt]/[Acid]) pH = 4.73 + log(0.50/0.50) pH = 4.73 + log(1) pH = 4.73 + 0 = 4.73

Conclusion: When [Salt] = [Acid], pH = pKa = 4.73. This confirms the Henderson relation — the buffer pH equals the pKa of the weak acid when concentrations are equal.

sqs.q: The Ksp of Ag₂CrO₄ is 1.12 × 10⁻¹². Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
sqs.a:
Dissolution equation:

Ag₂CrO₄(s) ⇌ 2Ag⁺(aq) + CrO₄²⁻(aq)

Let S = molar solubility:

[Ag⁺] = 2S, [CrO₄²⁻] = S Ksp = [Ag⁺]²[CrO₄²⁻] = (2S)²(S) = 4S³ 4S³ = 1.12 × 10⁻¹² S³ = 2.8 × 10⁻¹³ S = (2.8 × 10⁻¹³)^(1/3) = 6.54 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³

Conclusion: Molar solubility of Ag₂CrO₄ = 6.54 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³.

lqs.title: Q7(b) — Buffer Solutions & Solubility Product (Chapter 9)
lqs.q: Write a detailed note on buffer solutions including types, preparation, working, and Henderson's equation. OR Discuss solubility product (Ksp) and its two main applications with examples.

parts.label: BUFFER SOLUTION — DEFINITION & FACTS
points: A buffer resists change in pH when a small amount of acid or base is added.
pH does not change on dilution and remains stable for a long time.
Works on principles of Le Chatelier's principle and common ion effect.

parts.label: TYPES OF BUFFER
points: Acidic buffer (pH < 7): weak acid + its salt with strong base. Example: CH₃COOH + CH₃COONa.
Basic buffer (pH > 7): weak base + its salt with strong acid. Example: NH₄OH + NH₄Cl.
Salt provides conjugate base (acidic buffer) or conjugate acid (basic buffer) — the common ion.

parts.label: BUFFER WORKING (ACIDIC BUFFER EXAMPLE)
points: CH₃COONa fully dissociates → large reservoir of CH₃COO⁻ (common ion).
When H⁺ is added: CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH — acid absorbed, pH unchanged.
When OH⁻ is added: CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O — base neutralized, pH unchanged.

parts.label: HENDERSON'S EQUATION
points: pH = pKa + log([Salt]/[Acid]) — derived from Ka expression.
When [Salt] = [Acid]: log(1) = 0, so pH = pKa.
Example: CH₃COOH/CH₃COONa with equal concentrations → pH = pKa = 4.74.
pKa controls the pH of a buffer when both components are equal.

parts.label: SOLUBILITY PRODUCT (Ksp)
points: Ksp = product of molar concentrations of ions raised to stoichiometric exponents at equilibrium.
Applies to sparingly soluble salts only. Strong electrolytes (NaCl) have no Ksp.
PbSO₄: Ksp = [Pb²⁺][SO₄²⁻]; Ca(OH)₂: Ksp = [Ca²⁺][OH⁻]².
Ksp is temperature-dependent only — NOT changed by adding common ions.

parts.label: APPLICATIONS OF Ksp
points: App 1 — Calculating solubility: Set up ICE table, express [ions] in terms of S, substitute into Ksp. For Ca(OH)₂: 4S³ = Ksp → S = (Ksp/4)^(1/3).
App 2 — Predicting precipitation: Calculate Qc from actual ion concentrations. If Qc > Ksp → precipitation. If Qc < Ksp → no precipitation.
Example: CaSO₄ (Ksp = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵). Mixing 5.0 × 10⁻³ M each: Qc = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ > Ksp → precipitates.
Common ion effect: adding common ion decreases solubility while Ksp stays constant.

lqs.title: DQ5 — Common Ion Effect: Applications
lqs.q: Discuss applications and implications of the common ion effect in various fields.

parts.label: DEFINITION AND PRINCIPLE
points: Common ion effect: suppression of ionization of a weak electrolyte by adding a common ion.
Based on Le Chatelier's principle — adding a product shifts equilibrium left.
Results in reduced ionization, lower ion concentrations, and increased un-ionized form (may precipitate).

parts.label: APPLICATION 1 — PURIFICATION OF NaCl
points: NaCl dissolved in water (brine) is treated with HCl gas.
HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻; Cl⁻ is the common ion with NaCl equilibrium.
Equilibrium shifts left: Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → NaCl(s). Pure NaCl crystallizes out.
Used industrially to produce high-purity sodium chloride.

parts.label: APPLICATION 2 — GROUP II SALT ANALYSIS
points: H₂S is passed through acidic solution (HCl present) to precipitate Group II radicals.
H⁺ from HCl is the common ion: suppresses H₂S ⇌ 2H⁺ + S²⁻ equilibrium.
Low [S²⁻] ensures only Group II cations (Cu²⁺, Cd²⁺, Sn²⁺) precipitate as sulfides.
Example: Cd²⁺ + H₂S → CdS↓ + 2H⁺.

parts.label: APPLICATION 3 — GROUP III SALT ANALYSIS
points: NH₄Cl is added to NH₃ (aqueous) before precipitating Group III cations.
NH₄⁺ from NH₄Cl is the common ion: suppresses NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻.
Controlled [OH⁻] ensures only Group III cations (Fe³⁺, Al³⁺, Cr³⁺) precipitate as hydroxides.
NH₄Cl + NH₄OH mixture is the Group III reagent.

parts.label: APPLICATION 4 — BUFFER PREPARATION
points: Buffer solutions use common ion effect to maintain stable pH.
CH₃COONa provides CH₃COO⁻ (common ion), suppressing CH₃COOH dissociation.
Blood uses bicarbonate buffer (HCO₃⁻/CO₃²⁻) to maintain pH ~7.4.
Medicines and injections are buffered to prevent dangerous pH changes in blood.

lqs.title: DQ6 — Solubility Product for Sparingly Soluble Salts
lqs.q: What is the solubility product for sparingly soluble salts? Give its two applications.

parts.label: DEFINITION AND DERIVATION
points: Ksp = product of molar concentrations of ions raised to stoichiometric exponents at equilibrium.
Applies to sparingly soluble salts where equilibrium exists between solid and dissolved ions.
Derived by incorporating constant [solid] into Kc: Kc × [solid] = Ksp.
For PbSO₄: Ksp = [Pb²⁺][SO₄²⁻]. For PbCl₂: Ksp = [Pb²⁺][Cl⁻]².
Ksp is temperature-dependent — does NOT change with concentration.

parts.label: APPLICATION 1 — CALCULATING MOLAR SOLUBILITY
points: Let S = molar solubility. Express [ions] in terms of S using the balanced equation.
For Ca(OH)₂: [Ca²⁺] = S, [OH⁻] = 2S → Ksp = S(2S)² = 4S³.
Solve: S = (Ksp/4)^(1/3). If Ksp = 6.5 × 10⁻⁶ → S = 1.18 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³.
Individual ion concentrations follow: [Ca²⁺] = S, [OH⁻] = 2S = 2.36 × 10⁻² M.
This method works for any sparingly soluble salt once the formula is known.

parts.label: APPLICATION 2 — PREDICTING PRECIPITATION
points: Calculate ionic product Qc from the actual concentrations of ions mixed.
Compare Qc with Ksp: Qc > Ksp → precipitate; Qc = Ksp → saturated; Qc < Ksp → dissolves.
Example: Mixing 5 × 10⁻³ M Ca²⁺ and 5 × 10⁻³ M SO₄²⁻: Qc = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵.
Ksp(CaSO₄) = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵. Since Qc > Ksp → CaSO₄ precipitates.
Used in analytical chemistry to selectively precipitate specific ions.

quiz.q: What is the value of Kw for pure water at 25°C?
In neutral water at 25°C, [H⁺] equals:
quiz.exp: In neutral water [H⁺] = [OH⁻]. [H⁺]² = Kw = 10⁻¹⁴, so [H⁺] = 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³.

quiz.q: Kw increases with temperature because water ionization is:
quiz.exp: Water self-ionization is endothermic. Increasing temperature shifts equilibrium right (Le Chatelier), increasing [H⁺] and [OH⁻], so Kw increases.

quiz.q: pH + pOH at 25°C always equals:
quiz.exp: pH + pOH = −log[H⁺] + (−log[OH⁻]) = −log(Kw) = −log(10⁻¹⁴) = 14.

quiz.q: What is the pOH of a solution with [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁴ M?
quiz.exp: pOH = −log[OH⁻] = −log(10⁻⁴) = 4.

quiz.q: A weak acid has Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. The acid is classified as:
quiz.exp: Ka < 10⁻³ indicates a weak acid. Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ << 10⁻³, confirming the acid is weak.

quiz.q: For a weak acid HA with Ka and concentration C, [H₃O⁺] ≈
quiz.exp: ICE table gives Ka ≈ x²/C (since x << C). Solving: x = [H₃O⁺] = √(Ka × C).

quiz.q: Henderson's equation gives pH = pKa when:
quiz.exp: pH = pKa + log([Salt]/[Acid]). When [Salt] = [Acid], log(1) = 0, so pH = pKa.

quiz.q: An acidic buffer is prepared from:
quiz.exp: Acidic buffer (pH < 7) = weak acid + salt of its strong base. E.g., CH₃COOH (weak acid) + CH₃COONa (conjugate base salt). pH < 7.

quiz.q: When OH⁻ is added to a CH₃COOH/CH₃COONa buffer, the pH:
quiz.exp: The weak acid (CH₃COOH) neutralizes the added OH⁻: CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O. pH changes only slightly — this is buffer action.

quiz.q: Which common ion suppresses H₂S ionization in Group II salt analysis?
quiz.exp: HCl provides H⁺. H₂S ⇌ 2H⁺ + S²⁻. Adding H⁺ (common ion) shifts equilibrium left, suppressing H₂S ionization and lowering [S²⁻].

quiz.q: Adding Na₂CrO₄ to saturated PbCrO₄ solution causes:
quiz.exp: CrO₄²⁻ is the common ion. Extra CrO₄²⁻ increases Qc above Ksp, shifting equilibrium left — more PbCrO₄ precipitates and solubility decreases. Ksp stays constant.

quiz.q: For Ca(OH)₂ dissolving as Ca²⁺ + 2OH⁻, the Ksp expression is:
quiz.exp: Ksp = [Ca²⁺][OH⁻]². The stoichiometric coefficient 2 for OH⁻ becomes the exponent. [Ca²⁺]¹ × [OH⁻]².

quiz.q: If Qc > Ksp for a salt solution, the solution is:
quiz.exp: Qc > Ksp means the actual ion product exceeds the equilibrium value → the solution is supersaturated and precipitation occurs to reduce ion concentrations back to Ksp.

quiz.q: Ksp of AgCl = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰. The molar solubility of AgCl in pure water is approximately:
quiz.exp: AgCl ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻. Ksp = S². S = √(1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.34 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³.

quiz.q: Adding NaCl to a saturated AgCl solution will:
quiz.exp: Cl⁻ from NaCl is the common ion. AgCl ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻. Extra Cl⁻ shifts equilibrium left — more AgCl precipitates and [Ag⁺] decreases.

quiz.q: The pKa of acetic acid (Ka = 1.85 × 10⁻⁵) is approximately:
Blood maintains a stable pH of ~7.4 using a:
quiz.exp: Blood uses a bicarbonate buffer (HCO₃⁻/H₂CO₃ system) to maintain stable pH ~7.4. It resists pH change due to added acids or bases from metabolic processes.

quiz.q: [H⁺] in 0.1 M HNO₂ (Ka = 4 × 10⁻⁴) is approximately:
What is the pH of a 0.01 M NaOH solution at 25°C?
quiz.exp: NaOH fully dissociates: [OH⁻] = 0.01 = 10⁻² M. pOH = −log(10⁻²) = 2. pH = 14 − 2 = 12.
